# The Census of Thirty, and Science Has No Subjects

## Thirty People

Bodri asks you to imagine every master from every spiritual school on earth put into one room — Tantra, Taoism, yoga, Sufism, Confucianism, Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism, Shinto, Jainism, Islam, all of them.

Then he counts.

> Only two or three of these people will have mastered the fourth dhyana attainment. About three or four more will have reached the stage of the third dhyana ... about seven or eight will have reached the second dhyana attainment as their highest stage of achievement. Lastly, only about sixteen to eighteen others can be said to have actually achieved the true first dhyana attainment.[^1]

Then he takes some of it back. Of those fewer than twenty at the first dhyāna, *over half will have reached only a mediocre attainment, which doesn't really rank as the genuine first dhyana*.

> That's only about **thirty people in the world** who have true dhyana attainments at present.[^1]

Thirty. On a planet of billions, across every contemplative tradition that exists.

And they are unavailable: *most of these individuals will remain unknown to the general public because they want to cultivate in peace.*[^1]

## Where Everyone Else Is

The census is not only a headcount. It comes with a diagnosis of what the rest of the world's serious practitioners have actually got, and the diagnosis connects to everything else in this cluster.

> Many are only halfway to the first dhyana, or have achieved some such stage of concentration that involves a mistaken entry into the du-yin shadow consciousness, the flip side of the sixth consciousness of discrimination.[^1]

And then the sentence that explains the entire landscape of spiritual claims on his account:

> That's actually what we usually find and accounts for why many individuals are psychic, but people mistake this for a definite attainment precisely because **it's easy to produce psychic powers in this state**.[^1]

So the modal outcome of serious practice, worldwide, is a mistaken entry into the image-faculty — which is easy to reach, produces impressive results, and looks from inside like arrival.

That is a coherent picture rather than an insult. It says the world is full of people with genuine, unusual capacities and almost nobody with the thing those capacities are supposed to indicate, and it names the specific wrong turn that produces exactly that distribution.

## The Argument Science Cannot Answer

The census exists to support a methodological claim, and the claim is better than the census.

> Scientists always want to study advanced cultivation students or well known yogis, but "advanced students" aren't even close to first dhyana attainments, and yogic masters are notoriously limited in their achievements! They only accomplish their special states through forced gong-fu rather than through real dhyana attainments.[^2]

The structure is a **sampling objection**, and as an objection it is sound.

If the states in question are real and are held by roughly thirty people, and if those people are unknown and uninterested in being studied, then research recruiting from meditation centres, retreat populations and publicly available teachers is sampling from a population that does not contain the phenomenon. **Null results from such a sample say nothing about whether the phenomenon exists.**

That is not special pleading. It is the ordinary problem of studying anything rare in a convenience sample, and it applies with full force to a research literature that has largely recruited whoever was available.

He states the consequence with an image borrowed from the tradition's parable of rare human birth:

> A scientist has as much chance of encountering someone with Tao as an ocean turtle has in randomly popping to the surface of the water with its head coincidentally sticking through a hole in a piece of floating wood.[^3]

## What the Arithmetic Says About Every Available Teacher

There is a consequence of the census that Bodri does not draw, and it follows from the numbers alone without adding anything.

If genuine dhyāna attainment is held by roughly thirty people, and if *most of these individuals will remain unknown to the general public because they want to cultivate in peace*,[^1] then the set of people who are **publicly available as teachers** and the set of people who **hold the attainment** barely overlap.

Run it forward. Anyone with a website, a sangha, a publishing schedule or a retreat calendar is, by this arithmetic, almost certainly outside the thirty. Not because they are dishonest — the census makes no such accusation — but because visibility and the attainment are, on his own account, negatively correlated by disposition.

That is a stronger claim than anything in the sampling objection, and it is aimed inward rather than at scientists. **The census does not merely say that researchers cannot find subjects. It says that practitioners cannot find teachers**, by the same arithmetic and for the same reason.

Which collides with the rest of the book in two places.

It collides with the argument that a practitioner needs a master with the right dharma eye to shorten their error-correction loop — because the arithmetic says such masters are essentially unobtainable, and the one thing the book identifies as the teacher's genuine function requires one.

And it collides, quietly, with the existence of the book. An author publishing six hundred pages on the stages of attainment is not cultivating in peace. Bodri does not claim membership of the thirty anywhere, and it is to his credit that he refuses to treat his own testimony as proof. But the census he prints classifies the entire visible field, and he is standing in it.

## Implementation Workflow

The census is not something you can act on. What you can act on is the thing underneath it, and it is worth separating.

**Take the sampling point seriously wherever you meet a study.** When a piece of research reports that meditation does or does not produce some effect, ask who was in the sample and by what criterion they were selected. If the answer is *people who volunteered from a retreat centre*, then the study is informative about that population and about nothing else. This is ordinary methodological hygiene and it does not require accepting a word of the surrounding metaphysics.

**And then run the objection in the other direction, which the passage never does.** If the sample cannot contain the phenomenon, the same is true of any positive result. A study finding remarkable capacities in convenience-sampled meditators is, on this argument, also studying the wrong people. The objection cuts both ways and is only ever deployed one way.

For your own practice the census has exactly one usable implication, and it is deflationary in a helpful direction. If genuine first dhyāna is held by something like a dozen living people, then **whatever you have is not that**, and the question of where you are on the ladder can be set down. What remains is the ordinary work, which was always the case.

The thing to watch for is the opposite reaction, which arrives easily: the census makes attainment so rare that it becomes glamorous, and glamour attaches to the person who thinks they might be an exception. A number this small is not an invitation to wonder.

## Analytical Case Study: Precision Without a Method

The census's most revealing feature is not its size. It is its **granularity**.

*Two or three* at the fourth dhyāna. *Three or four* at the third. *Seven or eight* at the second. *Sixteen to eighteen* at the first. And then a correction — *over half* of the last group discounted as mediocre — producing a total of about thirty.[^1]

Those are not round numbers. They are the numbers of somebody who has counted.

And there is no method anywhere. Not a hint of how the enumeration was performed, what would count as evidence that a given person holds the third dhyāna, who was assessed, or how someone who is by stipulation unknown and uninterested in being found was included in the tally.

**This is a specific failure and it is worth naming precisely, because it is not the same as being wrong.** A vague claim — *very few people reach these states* — would be modest, unfalsifiable and unobjectionable. The bracketed counts convert the same unfalsifiable claim into something that reads like a survey result, and the reading is entirely produced by the format.

Two further observations, in fairness to the source.

**The internal structure is at least consistent.** The numbers form a plausible pyramid, each tier smaller than the one below, with the largest attrition at the entry level. Whatever generated them, it was not carelessness.

**And there is an implied method, though it is never stated.** Bodri's tradition holds that a practitioner at a sufficient level can survey and assess others — a claim he makes explicitly elsewhere about knowing who is who. If that is the census's basis, it would explain both the confidence and the absence of stated method, since the method would not be communicable. It would also make the census a claim that only the person making it could evaluate, which is where this cluster keeps arriving.

## The Structure That Forecloses Disconfirmation

Put the census and the sampling objection together and look at the shape of the resulting position.

The phenomenon is held by about thirty people. Those people are **unknown by preference**. Anyone available to be studied is, by that availability, probably not one of them. And practitioners who fail to demonstrate the states are evidence of nothing, because they were never the right subjects.

**No possible study can produce a result that counts against the claim.** A negative finding is explained by the sample. A positive finding would be welcomed. And the population that would settle it has been defined as unreachable.

Bodri does state what would resolve it — *if they really wished to prove these abilities without contest, they would have to seek out accomplished cultivation adepts with true dhyana attainments*.[^4] But that instruction cannot be followed by the people to whom it is addressed, since finding such a person requires the capacity to recognise one, which is precisely what the research would be trying to establish.

It is worth being fair about what this is and is not. **It is not a trick.** The sampling problem is real, and if the phenomenon exists it would genuinely be very hard to study. A rare, private, self-concealing capability is a difficult research object under any epistemology.

But the difficulty and the immunity are the same fact seen from two sides, and the passage takes only the first view. A claim that cannot be tested because its subjects hide is in the same evidential position as a claim with no subjects — and nothing in the argument distinguishes the two cases.

## The Decline Claim, and the One Testable Assertion

The census is given a historical dimension, and the two halves of it are of very different quality.

**The unfalsifiable half.** In ancient times *these counts would be much higher*, because *in earlier times people's minds were much less busy than our own*.[^1] That is the standing decline narrative, with a mechanism attached that cannot be checked — nobody has a measurement of how busy tenth-century minds were.

**The half with a testable shape.** Shakyamuni, he says, *produced many students who had extremely high samadhi attainments, and who were able to achieve self-realization during his lifetime*, and this is what makes his teaching *extraordinarily unique*: **search any other school and you'll find no other comparable track record.**[^5] Only the Zen school, with masters such as Ma Tsu, offers *even a modicum of resemblance*.

That is a partisan claim and it is also, in principle, a claim about the documentary record. Traditions do record how many of a founder's contemporaries were held to have attained. Whether the Buddhist record is exceptional in this respect is a question that could be argued from sources, and Bodri does not argue it — he asserts it and moves on.

And the modern coda is the harshest thing in the passage: not merely that few have awakened, but that *we don't just have people who mislead themselves in this area, but we have people who also go out of their way to lie about this to others*.[^5]

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support.** The sampling objection is methodologically sound and does not depend on the census being right. If a capacity is rare and its holders self-concealing, convenience samples cannot speak to it — which is a real limitation on a real research literature.[^2]

**The tension the source does not close.** The sampling objection is deployed only against negative findings. It applies with identical force to any positive result from the same populations, and that direction is never run.

**A second tension, and it is the page's centre.** The census is granular to the individual — two or three, seven or eight, sixteen to eighteen — and no method of enumeration is stated or implied in the text.[^1] Precision of that kind ordinarily signals a count; here it can only signal confidence.

**A third.** The position is structurally immune to disconfirmation: the subjects who would settle it are defined as unavailable, and the capacity to identify them is the thing in question.[^4] Whether that is a feature of a difficult research object or of an untestable claim, nothing in the passage distinguishes.

**A fourth, on the decline claim.** *Earlier minds were less busy* is offered as the mechanism for a higher historical count and cannot be checked.[^1] `[SINGLE SOURCE]`

**And the standing scope limit.** The dhyāna attainments being counted are, by footnote 518, stations on a ladder the author calls false stages.[^6] A world census of a rest stop is a strange object, and the source does not remark on it.

**Open questions.** Is the track-record claim arguable from sources — does the Buddhist record of contemporary attainments actually stand out against other traditions', and what would count as evidence either way? And is there any research design that could address a rare, self-concealing capability, or is that combination simply outside what empirical method can reach?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/du-yin-and-the-psi-programmes|Du-Yin and the Psi Programmes]], this page supplies the population statistics for that page's mechanism. There, the image-faculty produces impressions unconstrained by sense input; here, mistaken entry into that faculty is named as what *most* serious practitioners worldwide have actually achieved. The two pages together make a strong claim: the global distribution of spiritual attainment is mostly a distribution of du-yin entries.

The convergence with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/verification-and-its-broken-chain|Verification and Its Broken Chain]] is the uncomfortable one. That page establishes that nobody can reliably certify attainment — not a master, not a committee, not the practitioner. This page produces a headcount of the attained, to the individual. **The census requires exactly the faculty the other page says does not reliably exist**, and the two passages are two hundred pages apart.

Read with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/superpowers-are-not-evidence|Superpowers Are Not Evidence]], the account is consistent and the consistency is worth crediting. Powers are easy to produce from the shadow consciousness; the shadow consciousness is where most practitioners end up; therefore the world contains many people with real capacities and almost nobody with attainment. Three separate claims, made in three chapters, that fit.

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/you-cannot-elect-a-saint|You Cannot Elect a Saint]], the tension is direct. That page's objection to canonisation is that attainment is a fact no committee can vote on, and that the evidence class does not discriminate. This page conducts a one-man global assessment of who holds what, on no stated evidence at all.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**Survivorship bias, running backwards** — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/teen-star-to-adult-star-survivorship-pattern|The Transition Most Child Stars Don't Survive]]. That page's discipline is the standard correction: for every visible success there is a longer quiet list of names who did not make it, and any estimate built from the visible cases overstates the odds because the failures are silent. Bodri's census inverts every term. Here it is the **successes** that are silent — the thirty remain unknown *because they want to cultivate in peace* — while the visible population consists of people the account classifies as having taken a wrong turn. **What the pairing gives that neither side gives alone: inverted survivorship is immune to the correction that fixes ordinary survivorship, and immune for a structural reason.** The standard fix is to go and find the missing cases: the failed child stars exist, are nameable, and can be counted once you look. A doctrine holding that the successes are hidden by their own preference supplies no such recovery path — there is no register to consult, and the concealment is part of the claim. **So the two biases are not mirror images in practice: one is a correctable sampling error, the other is a sampling error that has been made uncorrectable by the same premise that asserts it.** Which is a useful general test — when someone explains a gap in the evidence by saying the good cases are invisible, ask what procedure would recover them, and notice if the answer is none.

*One handshake.* A second — a proxy standing in for an unobservable — is carried repeatedly elsewhere in this cluster and would be restatement here.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** **The sampling objection is sound and is only ever pointed at negative findings — while the census it supports is granular to the individual and rests on no stated method at all, which means the passage applies rigorous scepticism to everyone else's evidence and none to its own.**

**Generative questions.**
- Is the founder track-record claim arguable from sources — does the Buddhist record of contemporary attainments genuinely stand out, and against what comparison?
- Is there any research design that can address a rare, self-concealing capability, or does that combination place a claim permanently outside empirical reach?
- When a gap in the evidence is explained by the successes being invisible, what recovery procedure is on offer — and how often is the answer none?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/du-yin-and-the-psi-programmes|Du-Yin and the Psi Programmes]] — the mechanism this census is a population count of
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/verification-and-its-broken-chain|Verification and Its Broken Chain]] — the faculty this headcount requires and that page says does not exist
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/superpowers-are-not-evidence|Superpowers Are Not Evidence]] — why the world is full of capacities and empty of attainment
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/you-cannot-elect-a-saint|You Cannot Elect a Saint]] — the objection to assessing attainment, made by the same author
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/samadhi-concentration-absorption|Samādhi: Concentration and Absorption]] — the attainments being counted
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/false-stages-and-the-footnote-that-says-so|False Stages, and the Footnote That Says So]] — the conventional status of the rungs in the census
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/teen-star-to-adult-star-survivorship-pattern|The Transition Most Child Stars Don't Survive]] — survivorship, and what happens when it runs the other way

## Footnotes

The room of masters, the tiered counts, the mediocre-attainment discount, the total of about thirty, the unknown-by-preference claim, the du-yin diagnosis for everyone else, and the higher ancient counts with the busier-minds mechanism. **No method of enumeration is stated anywhere.** `[SINGLE SOURCE]` `[LOW CONFIDENCE]` as a claim about the world. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`
[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/bodri-various-stages-of-the-spiritual-experience|Bodri, The Various Stages of the Spiritual Experience]] — pp 359–360. The sampling objection: advanced students not close to first dhyāna, yogic masters limited to forced gong-fu. No study, researcher or programme is named. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`

the-five-liberations-refused.content:

domain: eastern-spirituality

# The Five Liberations Refused

## Offered All Five, They Take None

Kapila has just described the motiveless grade of devotion — the mind flowing toward him like the Ganges toward the ocean, without any purpose.[^1] The next sentence tests it:

> **Even if salokya, sarshti, samipya, sarupya and ekatva are offered, such people who are devoted to me do not accept anything other than service to me. This is said to be the extreme form of bhakti yoga**, where one transcends the three gunas and attains my state.[^2]

Debroy names them:

> Respectively, **residence in the same world as Vishnu, powers like Vishnu, residing near Vishnu, forms like Vishnu and union with Vishnu.**[^3]

Five liberations. Every one declined.

## What Is Being Turned Down

Read the five as a set and they exhaust the available goods.

**Sālokya** — the same world. Vaikuṇṭha, permanently.
**Sārṣṭi** — comparable powers. The capacities of the deity.
**Sāmīpya** — proximity. Being near him.
**Sārūpya** — the same form. Four arms, dark blue, yellow garments — the condition the volume describes the residents of Vaikuṇṭha as already occupying.[^4]
**Ekatva** — union. The end of being separate.

Place, power, nearness, likeness, merger. There is nothing a devotional system could offer that is not on that list.

**And the answer is *no* to all five, without ranking them.** The passage does not say the first four are acceptable and the fifth is not, which is the reading the later tradition sometimes gives it. It says such people *do not accept anything other than service to me*.

## The Counter-Offer

What they hold out for is one word: *service*.

Not a sixth reward. Not a better version of the five. A *relation* — and specifically the relation in which they are already engaged.

Which is why the refusal is coherent rather than perverse. Each of the five would change their position: move them, empower them, bring them closer, make them alike, or dissolve them. Service is the only thing on the table that leaves them where they are, doing what they are doing.

**They are not declining rewards in favour of a better reward. They are declining a change of state in favour of continuing.**

## Analytical Case Study: Why It Follows From Having No Motive

The refusal is placed immediately after the *nirguṇa* description and the placement is the argument.

A motivated devotee — any of the three graded kinds — has a reason for the practice, and a reward that satisfies the reason would end it. The *rājasa* devotee pursuing prosperity accepts prosperity and stops. That is what a motive is for.

The *nirguṇa* devotee has no reason. The mind flows toward him the way water runs downhill, and nothing in that arrangement is waiting to be satisfied.

**So there is nothing an offer could complete.** The five liberations are answers, and the motiveless devotee is not asking a question.

That is why the passage does not need to argue for the refusal or praise it. Having described a devotion without motive, the refusal is simply what follows — and the text marks it not as heroism but as a *definition*: *this is said to be the extreme form of bhakti yoga*.

**Register: this is a reading of the placement, one sentence after the *nirguṇa* grade.** The text supplies both and does not state the inference. What can be shown is the adjacency and that the refusal is described as the extreme form rather than as a choice.

## Ekatva Is the Hardest Refusal

Four of the five are goods. The fifth is not obviously a good and is not obviously refusable.

*Ekatva* — union — is what most of the traditions this volume is in conversation with treat as the terminus. Declining it is declining liberation in the strict sense.

And the passage does not soften it. It does not say union is inferior, or that the devotee will receive something better, or that the refusal is temporary. Union is listed fifth, in the same sentence, and refused with the rest.

The Second Skandha supplies the mechanism that makes this intelligible. The departing yogi who takes the highest route dissolves — *unites his atman and subtle form with water and slowly thereafter with fire, energy and wind* — and the volume is explicit that what ends there is the one who was looking.[^5]

**So refusing *ekatva* is refusing to stop being someone who can serve.** The relation requires two parties, and union supplies one.

## What the Refusal Costs

Worth naming, because the passage does not.

A devotee who declines all five remains in the condition of serving — which means remaining, in some sense, *available* to whatever the condition of a servant involves. The volume's other passages about that condition are not uniformly comfortable: the Brahmaloka residents have three hundred trillion years of anxiety at the sight of those who do not know the path,[^6] and Jaya and Vijaya were doorkeepers.[^7]

The passage does not raise this. It states the refusal as the extreme form of bhakti yoga and moves directly into a list of practices — image-worship, chanting, respect for the great, compassion for the poor.[^2]

**The most exalted position in the scheme is described as a job, and the text does not pause on what the job involves.**

## What Immediately Follows Is Extremely Ordinary

The sentence after the refusal is the one that changes how the whole passage reads:

> One must be immersed in the greatness of one's own dharma and **perform action without any motive.** One must always be engaged in the auspicious rites, **without any excessive violence.** Beholding my image, seeing it, touching it, worshipping it, praising me and chanting about me, he must be non-attached and based on sattva, **see me in all creatures.** He must show **a great deal of respect to the great, compassion towards the poor, friendship towards those who are equals** and practise yama and niyama. He must **hear about adhyatmika matters, chant my names, be upright, associate with noble people** and be without any kind of ahamkara.[^2]

Look at that list against what precedes it.

A being has just declined residence in Vaikuṇṭha, powers equal to the deity's, proximity, likeness and union — the entire inventory of what a cosmos can award. And the very next instruction is: be respectful to your seniors, kind to the poor, friendly to your equals, and do not be violent.

**Nothing in the list is exalted.** *Without any excessive violence* is a floor, not a summit. *Friendship towards those who are equals* is ordinary decency.

And *without any motive* appears in the second clause — the same phrase that defines the *nirguṇa* grade, now attached to *perform action*. So the motiveless condition is not a state achieved instead of practice; it is a *manner* in which entirely conventional practice is conducted.

Which reframes the refusal considerably. The person who declines five liberations is not thereby somewhere else. They are, by the next sentence, someone who chants, touches an image, respects the great and refrains from violence — the same activities available to a *rājasa* devotee pursuing prosperity in a temple.

**The difference between the highest grade and the second-lowest is not what is done.** It is whether anything is outstanding, and the passage makes that point by giving both the same to-do list.

And the claim itself is stated once. This is the volume's signature doctrinal claim in its primary-text form, and it occupies one sentence.

There is no elaboration, no example, and no character in the four Skandhas who is shown refusing a liberation. The claim is delivered by Kapila to his mother, in a discourse, as one line in a longer answer about the kinds of bhakti yoga.

Which is characteristic. The volume's widest claim about who can be reached is an epithet inside a bow;[^8] its identification of the deity with the refugeless is a clause in an apology;[^9] and its most distinctive soteriological position is a subordinate construction — *even if... are offered*.

**The Bhāgavata's most-cited positions are consistently the ones it states in passing and never develops.**

## Implementation Workflow: Recognising an Offer That Ends the Thing

You are offered something that resolves what you have been doing — a promotion out of the work, an acquisition, a settlement, a title that concludes the argument.

The five liberations are a taxonomy of such offers and it is worth having.

**Sort the offer by what it changes about your position.** Place, power, proximity, likeness, dissolution. Almost every completing offer is one of those: move somewhere better, get more capacity, get closer to the centre, become like the thing you admired, or merge into it. Naming which one clarifies what you are actually being asked to trade.

**Then ask what you would stop doing.** The refusal here is coherent because service is an *activity* and all five offers are *states*. If accepting would convert an ongoing relation into an achieved condition, you are being offered an ending, whatever it is called.

**And notice whether you have a motive left.** This is the passage's real test. If you have a reason for what you are doing, the right offer will satisfy it and you should probably take it — that is what motives are for, and declining a reward that answers your reason is not integrity, it is confusion. The refusal only makes sense from a position where nothing is outstanding.

Which means the honest question is not *should I refuse* but *is there anything here that an offer could complete*. Most of the time there is, and the answer is yes.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**The strongest evidence that the refusal follows from motivelessness rather than from valuation is its placement.** It is the sentence immediately after the *nirguṇa* description, and it is named as the extreme form of the same practice rather than as a separate virtue.

**Tension — the five are refused without ranking, including *ekatva*, in a corpus whose neighbouring traditions treat union as the terminus.** No justification is offered and none of the five is described as inferior. **Preserved.**

**Tension — the volume's most distinctive soteriological claim occupies one subordinate clause and is never illustrated by any character.** **Preserved unresolved.**

**Open question.** *Do not accept anything other than service to me.* Is service here a state the devotee is already in, or a sixth thing being requested? The reading determines whether the refusal preserves a condition or asks for one.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

This vault's Gauḍīya material treats this as the tradition's defining position — *mukti* subordinated to *bhakti*, the four lesser liberations sometimes tolerated and *sāyujya* consistently refused, with a developed apparatus explaining why.

The primary text supplies none of the apparatus. It gives five names in a list, refuses them together, and calls the refusal the extreme form. The distinction the later tradition draws between the four and the fifth is not made here.

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/everyone-in-vaikuntha-looks-like-him|Everyone in Vaikuṇṭha Looks Like Him]] documents the Second Skandha showing *sārūpya* in operation — residents with the deity's own form, dark blue and four-armed, and a household with servants and roles. Read against this refusal, that passage is a picture of the fourth item being accepted, by beings the volume nowhere criticises for accepting it.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**With [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/three-motivations-pleasure-power-meaning|Three Motivations: Pleasure, Power, Meaning]].** That page works a taxonomy of what drives sustained effort, with the three being genuinely distinct and the analytical payoff lying in identifying which one a person is actually running.

The five liberations map onto it with unsettling precision. *Sālokya* and *sāmīpya* are pleasure-shaped — better location, better proximity. *Sārṣṭi* is power. *Sārūpya* and *ekatva* are meaning at its limit — becoming, and being absorbed into, the thing that matters.

**What the pairing produces:** motivational taxonomies are built to *find* the driver, on the assumption that everyone has one and that naming it improves the fit between a person and their work. This passage supplies a case the assumption cannot cover: a category defined by having none of the three, whose behaviour is nonetheless sustained indefinitely. And the diagnostic consequence is sharp. A taxonomy of drivers cannot distinguish an unmotivated devotee from a person who is concealing their driver or has not identified it — both present as *none of the above*. Which means the framework's most useful application may be inverted: not sorting people into three boxes, but noticing when someone's behaviour survives the satisfaction of every driver you can name, because that is either the rarest case in the scheme or the clearest sign you have misread them.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The five exhaust what a devotional system can offer — place, power, nearness, likeness, merger — and the position the volume calls extreme declines all five in favour of continuing. Which makes the tradition's highest state not an attainment but a *refusal to be concluded*, and the only thing that makes such a refusal coherent is having had no reason for any of it in the first place.

**Generative questions.**

1. The passage refuses all five without ranking. Does the volume anywhere distinguish *ekatva* from the other four?
2. No character in the four Skandhas is shown refusing a liberation. Is the claim illustrated anywhere in the corpus?
3. *Nothing other than service.* Does the volume describe what service consists of for someone in this position?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/four-grades-of-devotion|Four Grades of Devotion]] — the description this refusal follows from
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/everyone-in-vaikuntha-looks-like-him|Everyone in Vaikuṇṭha Looks Like Him]] — the fourth liberation, shown in operation
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-one-grief-allowed-in-a-place-without-grief|The One Grief Allowed in a Place Without Grief]] — what the served condition contains
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/a-chain-of-praise|A Chain of Praise]] — the volume's habit of stating its widest claims in passing
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/krsna-bhakti-hub|Kṛṣṇa Bhakti Hub]] — the surrounding territory

## Footnotes

[^1]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/four-grades-of-devotion|Four Grades of Devotion]] — the nirguṇa description.
[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/debroy-bhagavata-purana-vol-1|Debroy, tr., The Bhagavata Purana Vol. 1]] — chapter 3(29), the five liberations refused and the practices that follow.
[^3]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/debroy-bhagavata-purana-vol-1|Debroy, tr., The Bhagavata Purana Vol. 1]] — endnote 1147, naming the five.
[^4]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/everyone-in-vaikuntha-looks-like-him|Everyone in Vaikuṇṭha Looks Like Him]] — the residents' form.
[^5]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-one-grief-allowed-in-a-place-without-grief|The One Grief Allowed in a Place Without Grief]] — the dissolution that ends the viewer.
[^6]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/debroy-bhagavata-purana-vol-1|Debroy, tr., The Bhagavata Purana Vol. 1]] — chapter 2(2), the exception clause.
[^7]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/let-us-not-forget-you|Let Us Not Forget You]] — the doorkeepers.
[^8]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/a-chain-of-praise|A Chain of Praise]] — the roster inside a bow.
[^9]: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/cows-and-brahmanas-are-no-different-from-me|Cows and Brahmanas Are No Different From Me]] — the identification claim.

# The Powerful Are Not Bound by Dharma

## Fire and Filth: The Doctrine With Teeth

Throw garbage on a fire. The fire eats it and stays clean. It doesn't catch the rot; it burns it. You could feed a bonfire a week of trash and at the end you have ash and heat, not a dirty fire. Fire takes in filth and gives back light, untouched.

That is the image the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* reaches for when somebody finally asks the obvious, dangerous question about Kṛṣṇa's night with the cowherd women. King Parīkṣit, listening to the story, stops the narrator cold. Kṛṣṇa came down, he says, to *protect* dharma — to uphold the moral order. He is its "original speaker, exemplar, and protector." So how could he touch other men's wives? That is the one thing dharma forbids most plainly. "He has performed an abhorrent deed. What was his purpose? Take away our doubt."[^1]

The answer the sage Śuka gives is not "he didn't really do it" and not "it was symbolic." The answer is harder and colder than that. "Just as fire consumes everything without being polluted, so it is seen that the blatant transgressions of dharma by the more powerful of rulers are not faults."[^2] The powerful — *īśvarāṇām*, those of sufficient spiritual mass — are like fire. They can take in the act that would defile anyone else and not be defiled. The rule that binds you does not bind them.

This is a doctrine with teeth, and the page you are reading exists to name both the teeth and the muzzle the text bolts on a single breath later. Because the very next verse slams the door: "One who is not a powerful being should certainly never behave in that fashion, not even in his mind."[^3] The exemption is real. It is also explicitly, deliberately non-transferable. And that combination — a genuine "beyond the rules" plus an iron lock against borrowing it — is exactly the structure that abusers and false gurus try to pry open. Hold both halves the whole way through. Drop either one and the doctrine becomes a weapon.

## What the Text Actually Claims

Strip it to the bone. The claim has two warrants and one fence.

The first warrant is ontological. It is about *what you are*, not what you do. Kṛṣṇa, in this telling, is "the Supreme Being of all Supreme Beings," the witness living inside the gopīs and their husbands alike, who "accepts forms according to his own will."[^4] His acts can't be measured against dharma the way yours can, for the same reason you can't fine the sun for shining on a thief. He is the source the rules flow from, not a subject inside them. The text generalizes this past Kṛṣṇa to a class — *īśvarāṇām*, powerful beings, even great sages "devoid of personal ego" who "do not accrue benefit through appropriate behavior, nor undesirable results through its opposite."[^5] Burn the ego out, and karma loses its grip; the deed no longer sticks to a self because there is no self for it to stick to.

That is the crucial mechanism, and it's worth saying slowly. The exemption is not a license to misbehave that comes with rank. It is the *disappearance of the one who would be bound*. Fire isn't being granted special permission to stay clean. Fire is clean by nature — there's no surface in it for the filth to settle on. The doctrine says the realized being is like that: no ego-surface, so no karmic residue. This is what separates the theologian's warrant from a tyrant's. The tyrant has a big ego and demands an exemption for it. The text's *īśvara* has burned the ego away, and the exemption falls out as a side effect.

The second warrant, layered on top, is devotional and pedagogical. Kṛṣṇa, the text says, "indulges in such pastime as a favor to the devotees. Hearing about these, one becomes fully devoted to him."[^6] The act is *līlā* — play, staged for love, not appetite. He "is content within himself," needing nothing, so the night is not lust filling a hole but overflow given as a gift.

Now the fence. "One who is not a powerful being should certainly never behave in that fashion, not even in his mind. Otherwise, acting out of foolishness, he will be destroyed; just as one who is not Śiva will be destroyed by drinking the poison churned from the ocean."[^7] That last line is the whole safeguard compressed into a single picture, and it deserves its own slow look.

## The Poison Test: Why the Exemption Won't Transfer

When the gods and demons churned the cosmic ocean, the first thing it coughed up was not nectar. It was *halāhala* — world-poison, enough to kill everything. Śiva drank it. He held it in his throat, which turned blue, and he lived, and the world lived. That is the whole point of the story: he could swallow what no one else could swallow, and survive.

So the *Bhāgavata* hands you the test. You want the exemption? Fine. Drink the poison. If you are Śiva, you live. If you are not Śiva, you die — "acting out of foolishness, he will be destroyed." There is no third option, no graduated dose, no "I'm a little bit Śiva." The capacity to absorb what would destroy an ordinary being *is the credential*, and it is not something you can claim. It is something the poison verifies, fatally, on the spot.

This is the genius of the safeguard, and it's why this page foregrounds it. The text does not say "only the worthy may do this" and leave "worthy" up for grabs. That would be an open door — every charlatan calls himself worthy. Instead it ties the permission to a test that *kills the unqualified*. The fire metaphor and the poison metaphor are the same claim seen from two sides. Fire: the one with sufficient mass takes in filth and stays clean. Poison: the one without it takes in the very same thing and dies. The act is identical. The agent's nature is everything. And the agent's nature is not self-certified — it is demonstrated by survival, which means by the time you'd know you qualified, you'd already be dead if you didn't.

Read this way, the exemption is wrapped in a hazard warning the size of the doctrine itself. "Never behave that way, not even in mind" is not a footnote. It is half the teaching. The Bhāgavata states the most antinomian thing a scripture can state — the realized are beyond the law — and in the same breath makes it the most dangerous thing a non-realized person could ever attempt.

## What This Gives the Vault

This page is the *theologian's* answer to a problem the vault already holds from the devotee's side. The gopīs' defense argues from below: love for God outranks duty to a husband, so the women who left their beds for Kṛṣṇa were not adulterers but the highest bhaktas — see the sibling [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/bhakti-transcends-dharma-the-gopi-defense|Bhakti Transcends Dharma: The Gopī Defense]]. That warrant runs *upward* — the devotee's love suspends the rule. This page runs *downward* — the agent's ontological status suspends the rule. Same scandal, opposite vector. One says love is bigger than dharma; the other says being is. Keep them distinct: confuse them and you'll think a strong feeling grants you the fire's immunity, which is precisely the error the poison test exists to kill.

It also gives the vault a clean instance of [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/god-beyond-morality-lila|God Beyond Morality: Līlā]] with the safety mechanism attached. Most "God is beyond good and evil" claims float free and get borrowed by anyone wanting cover. This one comes pre-fenced. That makes it a load-bearing reference for any later page touching antinomian licensing — the page you cite when you need the doctrine *and* its lock in one place.

## Analytical Case Study: Parīkṣit's Objection and Śuka's Answer

Look closely at how the dialogue is built, because the structure is the argument.

Parīkṣit doesn't ask a naïve question. He sets a trap with theology in it. He establishes that Kṛṣṇa "descended into the world for the establishment of dharma, and for the suppression of adharma," then names him the "original speaker, exemplar, and protector of the injunctions of dharma."[^8] He has stacked the case: the very being whose job is upholding the moral law has done the act that most flagrantly breaks it. This is not a believer's soft question. It is the sharpest objection the tradition can raise against itself, and the *Bhāgavata* raises it on purpose, in the king's own mouth. That matters. The scripture is not dodging the scandal; it is staging it at full strength so the answer has to be load-bearing.

Śuka's reply moves in a precise order, and the order is the safeguard. He leads with the fire — the exemption, stated boldly, no hedging. Then *immediately*, before the reader can run off with it, the poison — the lock. Only after both are nailed down does he give the deeper grounding: the egoless accrue neither merit nor demerit; Kṛṣṇa is the supreme witness who takes forms at will; the act is a favor to devotees that turns hearers into bhaktas.[^9] Notice the sequence. Permission, then prohibition, then explanation. If he'd given the explanation first, a reader might feel they understood the principle well enough to apply it. By front-loading the lethal warning, the text makes sure no one walks away with the permission unguarded.

And watch the final move. The chapter closes by *removing the scandal's residue without removing the scandal*. "Confused by his power of illusion, the menfolk of Vraj were not resentful of Kṛṣṇa; each thought his own wife was present at his side."[^10] No husband was wronged in his own experience. Then the moral payoff: "the sober person endowed with faith should hear and describe these pastimes... Achieving supreme devotion, one quickly frees oneself from lust, the disease of the heart."[^11] The story whose surface is maximal sensual indulgence is prescribed as a *cure for lust*. That inversion is the tell. The text never claims the act was ordinary. It claims the act, rightly heard, burns lust out of the listener the way fire burns the filth fed to it. The reader who treats the story as permission for their own appetite has read it exactly backward — they've drunk the poison thinking they were Śiva.

## Recognizing the Counterfeit: A Scene

Picture the room. A teacher sits at the front, devotees on the floor. He has done something that, done by anyone else here, would be called exploitation — and someone, finally, asks about it. The room tenses.

He smiles. "Fire is not stained by what it burns," he says. "The realized act for reasons you cannot see. Who are you to judge the play of a master?" Heads nod. The questioner feels small, sees the doctrine deployed, and goes quiet. The exemption has just been borrowed.

Now run the test the *Bhāgavata* actually demands, and watch it come apart. The text doesn't say "the master is beyond judgment, so stop asking." It says the opposite about *who may invoke this*: "never behave that way, not even in mind." The exemption is something the doctrine forbids you to *claim* — it is recognized in beings "devoid of personal ego," and the surest sign of ego is a man citing his own egolessness to license his appetites. The counterfeit always points the fire metaphor at himself and quietly drops the poison verse. The genuine article, if it existed, would be the last to reach for the exemption, because reaching for it is what an ego does.

So the diagnostic is sharp and usable. When you hear "the powerful are not bound by the rules," ask one thing: *who is saying it, and about whom?* If the powerful person is invoking it to cover their own act, the doctrine has been inverted — the text reserves the claim for *others'* recognition of a being "satisfied by worshipping the dust of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet,"[^12] never for self-exemption mid-transgression. The man drinking the poison and announcing he is Śiva is, by the text's own logic, already dying. He just hasn't noticed yet. And the room that nods along is helping him pour.

## Evidence, Tensions, and the Door Left Open

Hold the tension open, because the text does. It genuinely asserts both: (1) the truly powerful are not bound by dharma — *real*, stated without hedge; and (2) no non-powerful being may ever borrow this, on pain of destruction. The *Bhāgavata* does not resolve these into comfort. It lets the exemption stand in full force and lets the hazard stand in full force, and the gap between them is where the danger lives.

The unresolved edge is this: the text gives no procedure for telling a true *īśvara* from a counterfeit *from the outside*, before the poison does its lethal sorting. The poison test works on the agent — drink and find out — but a devotee in the room cannot administer it to the teacher. So the safeguard that is airtight in principle (only the genuinely realized survive) has a soft seam in practice (you can't run the test on someone else in real time). Bryant, writing as both Indologist and Gauḍīya practitioner, presents the doctrine as the tradition holds it; this is the tradition's position, documented, not endorsed.[^13] The vault's job is to mark the seam plainly: history is full of men who claimed the fire's immunity and were never made to drink. The doctrine's internal logic condemns them. Its practical application could not stop them. That gap is not a flaw to be smoothed over — it is the live wire, and the reason "never, not even in mind" has to be read as the loudest line in the passage, not the quietest.

One more open tension worth keeping: the text grounds the exemption in *egolessness*, but the same verses are spoken of Kṛṣṇa as supreme God, who has the ultimate "self" in the sense of being the cosmic person. Is the warrant "no ego, so no karma," or "the source of dharma cannot be judged by dharma"? The passage runs both arguments at once and does not separate them. For a sage like the ones it mentions, the first applies. For Kṛṣṇa, the second. A reader who collapses them — claiming the source-of-dharma exemption while plainly having an ego — has merged two warrants the text keeps in tension.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Bryant is, for now, the only source on this exact passage, but the doctrine sits squarely between two of the vault's standing voices on God-beyond-morality, and the contrast sharpens what's at stake.

Bryant, reading the *Bhāgavata*, makes the exemption *ontological and fenced* — it's about what Kṛṣṇa and the egoless sages *are*, and it comes welded to the poison warning. Set that beside the vault's handling of [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/lila-the-universe-as-divine-play|Līlā: The Universe as Divine Play]], where divine action is play without need, beyond the moral calculus that governs needy creatures. Both are saying the same structural thing: God's acts can't be scored on the human moral sheet because God isn't playing the game humans play. But where the līlā reading tends to dissolve the moral problem into aesthetic delight — it's all play, relax — Bryant's passage refuses to let it stay pretty. It drags the scandal back in through Parīkṣit's mouth and answers it with a death-threat to imitators. The tension reveals something the soft līlā reading misses: a doctrine of divine freedom is only safe when it comes with an explicit lock against human borrowing. Play, by itself, invites the appetite to call itself play. The poison verse is what keeps līlā from being a charlatan's alibi.

There's a quieter convergence with the vault's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/nonsectarian-bhakti-and-the-objectivity-of-mystical-vision|Nonsectarian Bhakti and the Objectivity of Mystical Vision]] strand. Both insist the realized state is a real ontological condition, not a self-report — vision is *objective*, exemption is *earned by being*, neither is something you grant yourself by sincerity. The implication neither states alone: the same move that protects mystical vision from "anyone who feels it sees truly" protects the dharma-exemption from "anyone who feels free is free." Self-certification fails in both. The state is verified by what it can do — see clearly, or drink poison and live — never by the claimant's confidence.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Here's the plain version of why a Sanskrit theology page shakes hands with the manipulation manuals and the psychology of self-deception: the exact logic the *Bhāgavata* states and then carefully locks — "the powerful are beyond the rules" — is the logic a cult leader states and deliberately leaves *unlocked*. The vault needs this page wired to those, so the theology carries its own antidote into the rooms where the doctrine gets weaponized.

- **Behavioral mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/authority-construction-belief|Authority Construction of Belief]] — The structure is identical; the safeguard is the difference. Both the *Bhāgavata* and the influence operator know that "this person is beyond the rules that bind you" is a massively powerful frame — it stops questions cold, as it stopped Parīkṣit's room would have, had Śuka not answered. The operator *manufactures* that frame to harvest compliance: build the leader's aura, then exempt him from the standards applied to everyone else, then watch followers stop checking. The *Bhāgavata* states the same frame but bolts the poison verse onto it precisely to stop the harvest — it forbids the claimant from invoking it. The insight that neither domain produces alone: the theological doctrine and the manipulation tactic are *word-for-word the same sentence*; what separates a tradition from a con is whether the sentence ships with the lock. A spirituality that says "the master is beyond judgment" and *omits* "and you may never claim this, on pain of death" has accidentally written a cult-recruitment script. The presence or absence of the poison verse is the diagnostic line between the two.

- **Behavioral mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/manipulation-technique-authority-costume|Manipulation Technique: The Authority Costume]] — The costume tactic dresses an operator in borrowed authority so targets defer without verifying. Map it onto the poison test and something snaps into focus: the costume is *exactly* the unqualified man drinking the poison while announcing he's Śiva. He wears the immunity without having the nature. The *Bhāgavata*'s fence is, functionally, a costume-detector — it says the credential is verified by capacity (survival, egolessness recognized by others), never by self-presentation. The insight: every "beyond the rules" claim splits into two and only two cases — earned immunity (verified by what you can absorb) and worn immunity (asserted by what you display). The theology insists only the first is real and makes the second lethal. The behavioral-mechanics page shows you how the second is built and sold. Read together, they give a single test for the guru-beyond-rules figure: *is the exemption something he survives, or something he wears?* See also the broader [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/guru-authority-transmission-theology-hub|Guru Authority and Transmission Theology Hub]] for where this lands in the vault's map of mediated authority.

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/self-deception|Self-Deception]] — The poison verse names a death that is usually slow and internal, not literal. "Acting out of foolishness, he will be destroyed" describes precisely the person who has convinced himself he is the exception. Self-deception is the engine: the man doesn't lie to followers first, he lies to *himself* — "ordinary rules are for ordinary people; my hunger is really love, really play, really teaching." Once that conviction sets, every transgression reads as license rather than damage. The *Bhāgavata*'s safeguard is, in psychological terms, a warning that the feeling of being the exception is the *least* reliable signal of actually being one — "devoid of personal ego" is something others recognize in you, never something you announce. Put the two fields side by side and here's what falls out: the subjective experience of exemption and the objective fact of exemption are not just different, they're *inversely correlated* — the loud inner certainty that one is beyond the rules is, by the text's own logic, the surest mark of someone who is not. Spiritual self-deception doesn't feel like deception; it feels like privileged access. That's why it's lethal, and why the door has to be locked from outside the deceived man's own judgment. (See also [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/spiritual-bypass-and-pitfalls|Spiritual Bypass and Pitfalls]] for how the "I'm beyond it" frame numbs the harm it causes.)

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

You probably read the poison verse as being about gurus and cult leaders — about *other* people borrowing an exemption they haven't earned. Turn it around. The doctrine says the surest sign you are *not* the fire is the feeling that you are. The moment you sense an inner permission — "the normal rules don't really apply to me here, I see deeper, my situation is special" — that very feeling is, by the text's logic, the poison already in your throat. Not metaphorically distant. Now. The exemption is recognized in beings who have burned the ego that *wants* an exemption; so the wanting is the disqualification. This cuts at the most flattering thought a developing practitioner has: *I'm advanced enough that the rules for beginners are loosening for me.* The Bhāgavata's answer is brutal and exact — if you can feel them loosening, you are precisely the one they must stay tightest on. Spiritual progress, on this reading, does not feel like earning exemptions. It feels like having less and less of a self that any exemption could belong to.

**Generative Questions**

- The poison test verifies the agent (drink and find out) but gives no tool to verify another person *before* the lethal sorting. Is that gap a flaw the tradition should have closed, or is the refusal to provide an external credential itself the safeguard — forcing communities to judge by fruits over time rather than by claimed status? An essay could argue the seam is a feature.
- Every robust antinomian doctrine across traditions seems to carry a lock (the poison verse here; "by their fruits" elsewhere; the tantric oath-bonds). Is there a general law — *no scripture safely states "the realized are beyond the law" without a non-transferability clause* — and can you find the traditions that stated it *without* the lock and trace what happened to them?
- The chapter prescribes the most sensual story in the canon as a *cure for lust*. What is the mechanism by which hearing about transcended appetite burns appetite out of the hearer — and is it the same mechanism the poison verse encodes, where the story can only "work" on someone who reads it correctly and would harm someone who reads it as permission?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/bhakti-transcends-dharma-the-gopi-defense|Bhakti Transcends Dharma: The Gopī Defense]] — the sibling warrant from below (love outranks duty); this page is the same scandal answered from above (being outranks duty). Read as a pair: two vectors, one exemption.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/god-beyond-morality-lila|God Beyond Morality: Līlā]] — the general claim this passage instantiates, here delivered with the poison-verse lock attached.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/madhurya-rasa-the-amorous-apex|Madhurya Rasa: The Amorous Apex]] — the rasa the rāsa-līlā embodies; this page handles the ethics problem that the amorous apex provokes.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-gopis-as-supreme-bhaktas|The Gopīs as Supreme Bhaktas]] — who the women were, theologically; this page asks how Kṛṣṇa's side of the same night escapes the charge of adharma.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/lila-the-universe-as-divine-play|Līlā: The Universe as Divine Play]] — play without need is the deeper ground beneath "the act was a favor to devotees, not appetite."
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/imposing-your-bhava-is-spiritual-violence|Imposing Your Bhāva Is Spiritual Violence]] — the vault's other check on devotional overreach; both insist that a real spiritual state is never something you assert over others.

[^2]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/edwin-bryant-bhakti-yoga|Bryant — Bhakti Yoga]] — Bhāgavata Purāṇa X.33.29 (the fire/īśvarāṇām verse), extract line 8555. [TRADITION].
[^3]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/edwin-bryant-bhakti-yoga|Bryant — Bhakti Yoga]] — Bhāgavata Purāṇa X.33.30 ("never behave that way, not even in mind"), extract line 8557. [TRADITION].
[^4]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/edwin-bryant-bhakti-yoga|Bryant — Bhakti Yoga]] — Bhāgavata Purāṇa X.33.33–35 (Supreme of Supremes; the supreme witness; accepts forms at will), extract lines 8563–8567. [TRADITION].
